title: Scaling idempotency: from a key table to dedup across regions and partitions
caption: Each stage removes the bottleneck of the previous one; switch the 📈 tabs to grow the system.
base_name: v1: keys in the inventory DB

steps.text: The key table sits next to the reservations, so claim, reserve and stored reply commit together. Nothing can be half done.
Good for a long time. It strains when key rows (one insert and one update per call, kept for days) outgrow the reservations and fill the primary's write budget and disk.

scenarios.name: v2: key store with TTL
scenarios.summary: Move keys to a dedicated, replicated key store that expires them on its own. The primary only writes stock; a unique constraint keeps duplicates out if the two ever disagree.

steps.text: Any API instance claims the key with a conditional write in the key store, which deletes keys once they are older than the longest retry.
The reservation commits in the inventory DB, then the reply is written back to the key. The primary no longer carries key traffic or cleanup.
Cost: key and reservation are no longer one transaction. A crash between them leaves the key in progress, so the unique constraint is the backstop and the store must be durable.

scenarios.name: v3: per-region keys
scenarios.summary: Each region has its own warehouses, stock and key store. A key belongs to the region that created it, so claims never wait on another continent.

steps.text: Orders reserve from the warehouses in their own region; claims and reservations stay local and fast.
Keys carry their home region as a prefix (eu_…, us_…), so the owner is known without a lookup.
Cost: a retry routed to the wrong region after a failover is forwarded home, at the price of one cross-region hop. Replicating keys everywhere would put that hop on every claim.

scenarios.name: v4: consumer dedup at scale
scenarios.summary: Partition the stream by order id so all events of one order reach one consumer, and give each partition its own seen-id table.

steps.text: The relay publishes with the order id as the partition key: every event for an order lands on the same partition, in order.
Each consumer writes the event id and the effect (a pick task) in one transaction against the seen-ids for its own partitions, so no global table is shared.
Cost: seen ids must outlive the stream's retention, or a replay processes old events again. Store them in daily partitions and drop whole days once they're older than retention.
